record_reviews.summary: The two retained body blocks are a public Darwin inquiry: he asks whether monoecious or dioecious flowers with sharply different sexes ever develop one sex in only half or a segment of the flower, paralleling insect gynandromorphy. The close is only his name, so no recipient or respondent is represented in the body. Footnote 1 dates publication to 10 February 1866; footnote 2 places the question against Darwin’s Variation work and says the editors supplied the only recorded reply, while footnote 3 points to Westwood’s insect examples.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Published in Gardeners’ Chronicle on 10 February 1866; XML [before 10 February 1866], 1809-01-01–1866-02-09. This is a later public query, not a dated 1851–55 exchange.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin is the sole surviving body voice. Editorial discussion of gynandromorphy, John Scott, Westwood, and the editors’ response is separate apparatus, not a letter from those people.

record_reviews.source_kind: preserved HTML public letter with full surviving body and scholarly apparatus
record_reviews.summary: Darwin’s three body blocks ask readers to examine Oxalis Bowei flowers and locate the stigmatic branches relative to inner and outer anthers. He reports his own plants as short-styled, asks for young long-styled or mid-styled flowers wrapped in tin-foil or oil-silk, and explains the purpose: cross-fertilising his plants to obtain seed. The closing supplies Down/Bromley but no named correspondent. The apparatus dates publication to 11 August 1866 and links the observation to his trimorphic Oxalis work and later Forms of flowers.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Published in Gardeners’ Chronicle on 11 August 1866; XML [before 11 August 1866], 1809-01-01–1866-08-10. Later than 1855; publication date does not establish an earlier receipt or prompt.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin’s body is an open appeal to readers; the cited Hildebrand correspondence, later Forms of flowers, and editorial species synonym are separate evidence layers.

record_reviews.source_kind: preserved HTML public letter with full surviving body and scholarly apparatus
record_reviews.summary: The three body blocks preserve Darwin’s experimental account rather than a correspondence reply. He reports failed crosses in peas, kidney beans, sweet peas, and Lupinus, attributes difficulty to early anther opening, stigma exposure, and possible repeated pollen application, then describes a paper cap filled with pollen. He records four successful Sweet Pea pods, four Lupinus pods, and one surprising Sweet Pea/Lathyrus grandiflorus cross, and generalises the cap method. Footnotes connect this public piece to his 1857–66 legume experiments and identify Gärtner’s earlier trials.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Published with 5188 in Gardeners’ Chronicle on 11 August 1866; XML [before 11 August 1866], 1809-01-01–1866-08-10. The later publication and cited 1849 book cannot establish 1851–55 knowledge or receipt.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin is the body author; reports of Dr Herbert, Gärtner, and Hooker are historical or cited voices, not incoming prompts.

record_reviews.source_kind: preserved HTML public letter with full surviving body and scholarly apparatus
record_reviews.summary: Darwin’s two body blocks ask the Gardeners’ Chronicle readership two linked questions: whether Knight himself raised Tall Blue and White Marrow peas, and whether seed saved beside other varieties ever produced crossed or “untrue” offspring. He contrasts the rarity he has observed with what pea fructification led him to expect and points to his striking dwarf-kidney-bean example. The footnotes date publication to 8 November 1862, identify Knight’s 1799 Philosophical Transactions paper, and correct Darwin’s body reference from 25 October to 24 October 1857.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Published on 8 November 1862; XML [before 8 November 1862], 1809-01-01–1862-11-07. Outside 1851–55; the 1857 kidney-bean reference is retrospective and cannot backdate the public query.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin is the sole body voice addressing anonymous readers; Knight and the prior Gardeners’ Chronicle paper are cited sources, not correspondents in this record.

record_reviews.source_kind: preserved HTML public letter with full surviving body and scholarly apparatus
record_reviews.summary: Darwin describes a natural-history observation in three body blocks: two purple-leaved rosettes appeared in a gravel walk five or six years earlier, vanished under trampling, and reappeared in the same spot to flower as Epipactis latifolia. He reconstructs the site’s former carriage-drive and pasture history, notes the orchid’s local rarity, and asks whether dormant rootstock or wind-borne seed explains it. Footnotes date publication to 15 August 1863 and identify later observations in DAR 70 and Orchids.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Published on 15 August 1863; XML [before 15 August 1863], 1809-01-01–1863-08-14. The five-to-six-year observation interval is internal natural-history timing, not a 1851–55 correspondence date.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin and his gardener are the eyewitnesses named in the body; the anonymous Gardeners’ Chronicle readership is the audience, with no preserved answer or named incoming source.

record_reviews.source_kind: preserved HTML public letter with full surviving body and scholarly apparatus
record_reviews.summary: Darwin’s two body blocks ask anyone owning an old gardening treatise or almanac to report the historical sowing date for scarlet runners or dwarf French beans, including title, date, and place of publication. His purpose is comparative: testing whether these plants can now be sown earlier than formerly. The footnotes identify the 8 October 1864 “Ancient Gardening” publication, connect it to his frost-resistance work in Variation, and record later replies that did not settle the question.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Published on 8 October 1864; XML [before 8 October 1864], 1809-01-01–1864-10-07. Outside 1851–55; later replies and Variation are retrospective publication context.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin is the body author addressing anonymous readers; later Frere, Buckman, Gould, and Dilke replies are identified editorially but are not preserved in this record.
